newsitem.title: UK: British business welcomes Labour's "new deal".
newsitem.headline: British business welcomes Labour's "new deal".

text.p: British business leaders on Tuesday welcomed the opposition Labour Party's pledge that it would not ditch sweeping trade union reforms made in the last 17 years if they win power in this year's election.
But lobby groups said businessmen and the party were still on a collision course over two key Labour policies -- a national minimum wage and the European Union's Social Chapter.
"We certainly welcome the Labour Party's willingness to stick with the trade union reforms," said Stephanie James, policy executive at the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC).
"Businesses are very happy with the industrial relations at the moment and will be very happy if a Labour government helps that continue."
But the BCC, along with other leading business groups, is still firmly opposed to a national minimum wage and employment legislation from the Social Chapter.

"There are still big problems with those two policies," said Ruth Lea, head of policy at the Institute of Directors. "We have not been swayed by any of Labour's arguments. We think they are wrong on those two issues and we will go on telling them."
An election is due by May. The ruling Conservative Party is well behind Labour in the opinion polls.
Labour leader Tony Blair pressed ahead with the party's campaign to win over the business community on Tuesday when he offered to form a new alliance with businessmen.

"Today I offer a new deal for the future. The deal is this: we leave intact the main changes of the 1980s in industrial relations and enterprise. And now, together, we address a new agenda for the 21st century -- education, welfare reform, infrastructure, leadership in Europe," he said.
Blair was addressing a business conference launching a new report on the future of British industry, written by the Commission of Public Policy and British Business.

The Commission, which includes a number of well-known industry chiefs, was set up by the left-leaning Institute for Public Policy Research. The report gave overt backing to some of Labour's key economic policies, such as the minimum wage.

Adair Turner, director general of the Confederation of British Industry, also addressed the conference. He said while the report was a very useful document, the CBI was still strongly opposed to a minimum wage.
"There are some recommendations on where approach differs, such as the call for the UK to sign up to the Social Chapter and the implementation of a national minimum wage."
Labour's pledge on trade union reforms comes a day after the party said it not raise income tax if it wins the election.
Industry groups have generally welcomed Labour's new pro-business policies and its extensive efforts to win their support has had some success.

The latest poll of managers' political allegiance conducted by the Institute of Management found that in November only 42 percent of managers backed the Conservatives, compared with 62 percent at the last election in 1992.
